title: No one stands the strict tribunal by inherent justice alone
source_text: XXXI. Porro cum justitia & sanctitas fidelium, seu quis habeat rationem virtutum quibus interius a Deo ornati sunt, seu bonorum operum quae inde promanant, & in qui-bus se exercent, imperfecta tantum & inchoata sit: nec solum illi sint in peccatis mortui, antequam Deus illos in gratiam recipiat: sed etiam post acceptam gratiam, variis lapsi-bus adhuc obnoxii maneant: certum est neminem, vi propriae justitiae, & bonorum suorum operum, posse coram severo tribunali Dei consistere, & ferre rigidum divini judicii examen; neque quemquam hominum damnationem vitaturum, & apud Deum infontem, & vita aeterna dignum pronunciandum fore, si Deus respiciat tantum ad ju-stitiam quae illi inhaeret, & bona illius opera, nec erga ipsum ulla indulgentia & cle-mentia uti velit, sed cum eo agere secundum legis praecise consideratae rigorem.
pass_a_gloss: Further, since the righteousness and holiness of believers—whether one has regard to the virtues with which they are inwardly adorned by God, or to the good works that flow from them and in which they exercise themselves—is only imperfect and begun; and since they were not only dead in sins before God received them into grace, but even after receiving grace remain still liable to various falls: it is certain that no one, by the force of his own righteousness and of his good works, can stand before God's severe tribunal and bear the rigid examination of divine judgment; nor will any man escape damnation and be pronounced innocent before God and worthy of eternal life, if God looks only to the righteousness that inheres in him and to his good works, and is unwilling to use any indulgence and clemency toward him, but to deal with him according to the rigor of the law precisely considered.
pass_b_english: Given imperfect inherent holiness and ongoing falls, no one can stand God's strict tribunal by his own justice and works alone.
Without indulgence, none would be cleared or judged worthy of eternal life.
